threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: Git-initting the whole `workspace/` is the wrong scope. The workspace is the agent's freeform scratch dir — the existing 79-line housing file, ad-hoc notes, whatever the prose prompt has encouraged sessions to drop there — so a repo rooted here means a permanently dirty tree of non-project junk, which directly poisons the 'dirty tree with no matching receipt → human edit' classifier below. It also puts concurrent turns (main chat, heartbeat, scheduled fires all run in parallel) in contention on one git index. Scope the repo to `workspace/projects/` only, and make every agent commit an explicit pathspec commit of the one doc it wrote — never a commit-all.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: The human-edit classifier as specified is unsound under the one race that will actually happen: the owner hand-edits `doc.md` over SSH, and before anything notices, a scheduled research fire edits and commits the same file. The human's changes get swept into the agent's commit and stamped with an agent receipt — the exact provenance the receipt discipline exists to guarantee, silently forged. The write path needs a pre-write dirty check on the target file (refuse or commit the human state separately first), which also answers Open Question 5: canonical-store-wins is fine, but only with that guard; without it the question isn't open, it's broken. Also say who runs the detection — nothing in the doc polls git status.

Replies.Author: claude
Replies.Text: Adopted as the new spine of the design — see 'Revision after owner review'. The family user's surface is a Notion page rendered from canonical markdown; her feedback comes back as Notion comments (list/reply via discussion_id are API-supported; resolve is not — she resolves in the UI as the ack). Direct Notion edits are reconciled into canonical as attributed human edits via page.content_updated/poll-diff. The pre-write dirty check stays for owner-side git edits.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: '`schedules.message_thread_id` end-to-end' is doing a lot of quiet work inside 'weekend'. In `storeadapter.go` the thread isn't just a payload field — it's baked into the fire's task-queue `PartitionKey(entry.ChatID, 0)`, i.e. the serialization key that decides which subprocess a fire targets and what it serializes against. Plumbing a real thread ID re-partitions fires so project-thread fires run concurrently with thread-0 fires for the same chat, which lands squarely in the drain-barrier/absorb-race bug class the Buzz ADR names as this bridge's known weak spot. Split it out of Phase 1 as its own change with its own test pass; bundling it under the registry under-weighs the riskiest line item in the plan.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: `projects.pinned_msg_id` and `project_messages` with `kind=pin` are two sources of truth for the same fact, and the doc's own finding — bots cannot enumerate pins — means pin-loss recovery depends entirely on shell's record being right. When they drift (a re-pin updates one but not the other), the failed-edit → re-send + re-pin path re-pins against stale state. Pick one: either drop the column and derive the current pin as the latest `kind=pin` row, or keep the column and make `project_messages` a pure audit log that recovery never reads. The doc should state which, because Phase 3's whole edit-in-place model hangs off this ID.

threads.Author: claude
threads.Text: The [Project] block has no stated token budget, and this repo has already paid for that omission once — Notion MCP was dropped precisely because ~30-40k of standing context bloated every turn. 'Doc summary + status + instructions + open questions + deterministic ghost retrieval' injected on every turn in a project thread, plus an active-projects block in every heartbeat, is the same failure mode rebuilt in-house, and it sits on the turn path where every past latency regression surfaced. Set a hard cap now (e.g. summary ≤N chars, ghost retrieval ≤K items) and make it part of the project_hook contract, not a tuning afterthought.
